headline: Xbox turns down Netflix's $500M offer for 7-year IP adaptation deal
summary: Netflix reportedly offered $500 million for exclusive rights to adapt Xbox characters over seven years. Microsoft countered with an $800 million demand, leading to the deal's collapse.
details: Netflix reportedly offered Microsoft $500 million for a seven-year deal to adapt Xbox characters into shows and films. However, Microsoft responded with a higher demand of $800 million, causing the deal to fall through.

Puck broke the news, detailing the negotiations. Xbox stated, "We have received record-breaking interest in our I.P.; Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations."
Microsoft is now reportedly shifting its strategy, pursuing "smaller deals with more partners" on a case-by-case basis. This moves away from an overarching exclusivity agreement with a single entity.

The tech giant has a history of successful media adaptations, including the live-action "Halo" series with Paramount, which ran for two seasons. They also have a "Call of Duty" film in the works at Paramount and a third season of "Fallout" at Amazon.

A sequel to "A Minecraft Movie" is set to open next year. Additionally, other popular Xbox titles such as "Gears of War," "The Elder Scrolls," and "Sea of Thieves" are currently being pitched for potential adaptations.
Netflix continues to invest in game-based content, with various works in production. This includes the animated "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," which recently returned for a new season.

topic: cerebras deploys trillion parameter ai models
headline_marked: [[Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models]] with 1000-2000+ tokens/sec throughput
headline: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models with 1000-2000+ tokens/sec throughput
summary: Cerebras details how its WSE-3T wafer-scale chips manage multi-trillion parameter models like Kimi K3 by splitting them across multiple wafers for extreme performance.
details: Cerebras has revealed how its WSE-3T wafer-scale chips are engineered to handle and deploy massive AI models. This approach enables the execution of multi-trillion parameter models at speeds of 1000-2000+ tokens per second.

The challenge lies in the memory requirements: a single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, while trillion-parameter models require terabytes for their weights. Cerebras addresses this by splitting large frontier models across multiple wafers.
As an illustrative example, Cerebras uses the open-source Kimi K3 model, which features approximately 3 trillion parameters. Kimi K3 is composed of 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.
Kimi K3 demonstrates frontier-level capabilities, scoring 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 91.2% on BrowseComp, outperforming some leading proprietary models on specific benchmarks.
Each layer of Kimi K3 requires about 16 GB of storage. This allows entire model layers to fit directly onto a single 44 GB Cerebras wafer, meaning model weights often remain stationary on the chip.

Model execution occurs in a pipeline, where the Cerebras compiler maps layers across wafer regions. The runtime then orchestrates the flow of tokens between wafers using RDMA over Ethernet, with only activations moving for ultra-fast latency.
The system avoids idle wafers by keeping the entire pipeline full with different requests simultaneously. Each wafer stage can process a distinct request at the same time, maximizing efficiency.
Furthermore, each stage can process micro-batches, which are small groups of requests. This design allows for a trade-off between faster individual request processing and increased total throughput.

The amount of on-chip memory dedicated to the KV cache dictates the maximum number of concurrent requests. Each active request requires its own KV cache on dense-layer wafers, setting a ceiling for simultaneous operations.
